title: What the Grid Hums

# What the Grid Hums

## The Background Electromagnetic Hum of GLMZ

The grid hums at 60 hertz. This has been true since the 20th century, when North America standardized its alternating current frequency, and it remains true in 2200 even though the power infrastructure has been rebuilt seventeen times. The base frequency persists like a genetic trait, inherited by each successive generation of technology from the one it replaced. Every transformer, every power conduit, every junction box in GLMZ vibrates at 60 hertz or one of its harmonics, and the sum of these vibrations produces a sound that is not really a sound — it is a presence, a tonal foundation beneath the city's acoustic life, so constant that the brain edits it out of conscious perception within hours of first exposure.

Different districts produce different harmonics. the Gray Zone's aging power infrastructure generates significant second and third harmonics — 120 and 180 hertz — from transformers that are overloaded and voltage regulators that have drifted out of specification. The result is a thicker, rougher hum, a sound with texture and character. The Circuit, with its heavy industrial load, adds a fifth harmonic at 300 hertz from the switching power supplies that feed its fabrication equipment. The Grind contributes a deep 30-hertz sub-harmonic from its high-capacity power distribution nodes, a frequency too low to hear but felt in the bones, in the teeth, in the way your vision subtly vibrates when you stand too close to a primary conduit.

Certain BCI models can hear the grid directly. The Axiom NeuroLink series from 2190 to 2197 had a firmware deficiency that allowed electromagnetic interference to couple into the auditory processing pathway, translating the grid's electromagnetic field into perceived sound. Axiom patched the issue in firmware update 4.7.2, but many the Gray Zone residents running unlicensed BCI firmware — either because they cannot afford updates or because they prefer unmodified systems — still hear the grid as a constant tone, pitched somewhere between a fluorescent light's buzz and a distant choir holding a single note. These users report that the tone changes character by location, and some have developed a navigation ability based on it — walking through the city by the sound of its electricity, following the hum the way a mariner follows stars.

The grid's voice changes before a blackout. Experienced the Gray Zone residents — particularly those with BCI models that render the electromagnetic spectrum as sound — report that the hum shifts pitch in the minutes before power loss. The frequency rises. The harmonics thin. The complex, layered sound of a healthy grid simplifies into a purer, higher tone as load-balancing systems fail and the remaining infrastructure strains to carry the full demand. The sound, they say, is like a voice going from speaking to screaming — the same source, the same fundamental character, but compressed into something desperate and singular. Then the hum stops. In the silence that follows, the Gray Zone holds its breath, and the only sound is the collective exhalation of a district that has just been unplugged from the 21st century.

There are places where the hum is wrong. Not absent — wrong. The Grind's western industrial corridor produces a hum that contains frequencies that do not correspond to any harmonic of 60 hertz. The anomalous tones have been measured at 73 hertz, 137 hertz, and 211 hertz — prime numbers, which should not appear in a system based on a 60-hertz fundamental. Engineers have traced the anomalous frequencies to a specific section of power conduit that runs beneath a building abandoned since 2180. The conduit carries current. The current produces hum. The hum contains frequencies that the current, according to everything known about electromagnetism, should not be able to produce. Maintenance crews avoid the corridor. They cite scheduling conflicts. They mean something else.
